audit.help.severity.info: Worth knowing, and worth a deliberate decision — not something you necessarily have to change.
audit.help.category.correctness: What is wrong: duplicate identifiers, parameters that go nowhere, examples their own schema rejects, constructs that contradict the declared OpenAPI version.
audit.help.category.security: What the document lets through: credentials or tokens sent in clear or in a URL, operations open without authentication, OAuth flows the security best practice forbids, secrets returned in responses, inputs with no size limit — each against the RFC or the OWASP risk it breaks.
audit.help.category.completeness: What is missing: operations, parameters, properties and request bodies with no description, responses with no example, an info block with nothing in it. Placeholder text — “TODO”, “string”, the name read back — counts as no description.
audit.help.category.deprecation: The inventory of everything marked deprecated, and whether each one says what to use instead or when it goes away.
audit.help.category.consistency: Whether the document keeps to its own conventions: naming of parameters, of properties and of path segments, and shapes written out inline instead of shared.
audit.help.category.readiness: What this documentation cannot do with this schema: unstable deep links, ungrouped operations, no environment to seed, no OAuth flow to run, prefilled requests generated for lack of examples.
audit.help.category.agent: What an AI agent calling this API through a tool gets from the schema: tool names the platforms accept, operations it can tell apart, inputs with a shape and values with a meaning, errors it can read — and what the MCP export cannot carry.
audit.empty.title: No findings.
audit.empty.hint: Every applicable check passes on this schema.
audit.annotations.omitted: {n} more finding(s) not annotated: GitHub shows ten of each kind per step. The full report lists every one.
audit.omitted.lessSevere: {n} less severe finding(s) not listed in this report.
audit.omitted.known: {n} finding(s) the baseline already accepts not listed in this report.
audit.rule.document-syntax.label: Invalid JSON or YAML
audit.rule.document-syntax.message: The file is not valid {format} at line {line}, column {column}: {detail}
audit.rule.document-syntax.why: Validators, code generators and most tools refuse the file outright. This documentation reads past the error to show what it can — a file that is not valid JSON is read as YAML, which accepts more — but what was meant there is a guess.
audit.rule.document-syntax.fix: Correct the text at line {line}, column {column}, then audit again: a parser stops at its first error, and another may follow.
audit.rule.document-openapi.label: Not an OpenAPI description
audit.rule.document-openapi.message: The file is no OpenAPI 3.x or Swagger 2.0 description: it holds {found}.
audit.rule.document-openapi.why: Nothing reads it as an API: this documentation refuses to render it, and so do validators and code generators. When the file is still a mapping, the rest of this report grades it as OpenAPI 3.2, the newest version.
audit.rule.document-openapi.fix: Make the file an OpenAPI description: a mapping whose openapi field names the version it is written in (3.0.4, 3.1.2 or 3.2.0). Convert a Swagger 1.x document to OpenAPI 3 first.
audit.rule.duplicate-operation-id.label: Duplicate operationId
audit.rule.duplicate-operation-id.messag: operationId “{operationId}” is used by more than one operation.
audit.rule.duplicate-operation-id.why: An operationId must be unique in the document, and this documentation turns it into the operation's deep link: one of the two links lands on the other operation.
audit.rule.duplicate-operation-id.fix: Rename one of the operationIds so that each value is unique in the document — a verb and a noun reads best (listPets, getPet).
audit.rule.path-param-declared.label: Path placeholder with no parameter
audit.rule.path-param-declared.message: The path uses “{name}”, which no parameter declares.
audit.rule.path-param-declared.why: The reader gets no field to fill it in, and the try-it sends the unfilled placeholder as part of the URL.
audit.rule.path-param-declared.fix: Declare a parameter named {name}, with in: path and required: true, on the operation or on its path item.
audit.rule.path-param-in-template.label: Path parameter absent from the path
audit.rule.path-param-in-template.messag: The path parameter “{name}” appears nowhere in the path.
audit.rule.path-param-in-template.why: It is rendered as a required field that goes nowhere — usually a rename that stopped halfway.
audit.rule.path-param-in-template.fix: Rename the parameter to match a placeholder of the path, add the placeholder to the path, or delete the parameter.
audit.rule.path-param-required.label: Path parameter not marked required
audit.rule.path-param-required.message: The path parameter “{name}” is not marked required.
audit.rule.path-param-required.why: The OpenAPI specification makes required: true mandatory on a path parameter. This app forces it anyway, but code generators and validators are entitled to reject the document.
audit.rule.path-param-required.fix: Add required: true to the parameter.
audit.rule.required-property-declared.la: Required property that is not declared
audit.rule.required-property-declared.me: “{name}” is required, but neither this schema nor the schemas it is composed with declare it.
audit.rule.required-property-declared.wh: The field is mandatory yet described nowhere, so the try-it form cannot even offer it. A name counts as declared when it is under the properties of the schema, of an allOf member, of a oneOf or anyOf branch, or of the schema this one is a branch or member of, or when a patternProperties pattern matches it. The names dependentRequired lists are read the same way.
audit.rule.required-property-declared.fi: Declare {name} under properties with its type, or remove it from the required list.
audit.rule.required-with-default.label: Required, and still carrying a default
audit.rule.required-with-default.message: “{name}” is required and still declares a default.
audit.rule.required-with-default.why: A value the caller must always supply never falls back to anything, so the default can never apply — and it says the opposite of required. Readers and code generators get contradictory signals about whether the field has to be sent.
audit.rule.required-with-default.fix: Remove the default — or, if the field really is optional, take it out of required (required: false on a parameter) and keep the default.
audit.rule.example-type-mismatch.label: Example contradicting its schema
audit.rule.example-type-mismatch.message: The example {value} breaks {keyword} of its schema at {at}.
audit.rule.example-type-mismatch.why: Readers copy examples and the try-it prefills requests with them, so a wrong one spreads into every client. The value is checked in depth: types, enums, lengths, patterns, bounds, sizes, required members, closed objects, compositions, and the common formats (dates and times, uuid, ipv4, ipv6, email, uri, int32, int64). The place is a path into the example, $ being the whole value. A request example does not owe a readOnly member, nor a response example a writeOnly one. A broken format alone is a warning: JSON Schema makes format an annotation by default, but readers and generated clients still trip on it.
audit.rule.example-type-mismatch.fix: Correct the example at {at} so that it satisfies {keyword} — or correct the schema if the example is the truth.
audit.rule.default-allowed.label: Default rejected by its own schema
audit.rule.default-allowed.message: The default {value} breaks {keyword} of its own schema at {at}.
audit.rule.default-allowed.why: The form prefills a value the API will refuse, and generators copy it as-is. The default is checked like an example: type, enum, lengths, pattern, bounds, sizes, members, compositions and the common formats. A broken format alone is a warning: JSON Schema makes format an annotation by default.
audit.rule.default-allowed.fix: Change the default so that it satisfies {keyword} at {at}, or widen the schema.
audit.rule.unused-component.label: Component never referenced
audit.rule.unused-component.why: A dead component documents nothing, yet it is downloaded by every reader and still has to be maintained.
audit.rule.unused-component.fix: Delete the component, or reference it with $ref from the place it was written for.
audit.rule.security-scheme-declared.labe: Security requirement on an undefined scheme
audit.rule.security-scheme-declared.mess: The security requirement names “{name}”, which components.securitySchemes does not define.
audit.rule.security-scheme-declared.why: The operation looks protected, but there is no scheme to build a credentials form from and no credentials are ever sent.
audit.rule.security-scheme-declared.fix: Define a scheme named {name} under components.securitySchemes, or correct the name in the security requirement.
audit.rule.response-substance.label: Response with nothing to say
audit.rule.response-substance.message: Response {status} has no description, and no content that says what it returns.
audit.rule.response-substance.why: It renders as a bare status line: the reader learns that the code exists and nothing else. A media type with no schema and no example — {"application/json": {}} — names a format and describes nothing; a file or plain-text type counts, its type says it all.
audit.rule.response-substance.fix: Give the response a description saying when it happens, and a content entry with a schema when it returns a body.
audit.rule.version-legacy.label: Superseded spelling in a newer document
audit.rule.version-legacy.message: {construct} is an older spelling, and this document declares OpenAPI {declared}.
audit.rule.version-legacy.why: A reader of the declared version ignores most of these spellings, and what they carried silently disappears: nullable no longer makes a field nullable, a boolean exclusiveMinimum is a type error, and x-nullable is a Swagger 2 extension no 3.x tool reads. Two are deprecated but still read, hence an info: a schema's example from 3.1 on, in favor of examples, and the XML attribute and wrapped booleans from 3.2 on, in favor of nodeType.
audit.rule.version-construct.label: Construct ahead of the declared version
audit.rule.version-construct.message: {construct} was introduced by OpenAPI {since}, and this document declares {declared}.
audit.rule.version-construct.why: This documentation reads it anyway, but a validator or a code generator trusts the declared version and is entitled to reject the document or drop the construct.
audit.rule.version-construct.fix: Raise the openapi field to OpenAPI {since} or later, or express it with what {declared} offers.
audit.rule.field-without-value.label: Field declared without a value
audit.rule.field-without-value.why: OpenAPI gives an empty value no meaning here, so the field says nothing. The usual cause is YAML: in a flow mapping, an unquoted comma ends the value — { description: The signed mandate, as uploaded } reads as the description “The signed mandate” and an empty field “as uploaded”, and the description shows cut short everywhere.
audit.rule.field-without-value.fix: Quote the text (description: "The signed mandate, as uploaded") or write the mapping in block style; if the field was meant to stay empty, delete it.
audit.rule.discriminator-mapping.label: Discriminator mapping pointing nowhere
audit.rule.discriminator-mapping.message: The discriminator maps {key} to {target}, which is none of the schemas it can dispatch to.
audit.rule.discriminator-mapping.why: A client reading this mapping cannot tell what shape {key} stands for. This documentation still shows the key, with nothing to expand behind it.
audit.rule.discriminator-mapping.fix: Point the mapping at one of the composite's variants, or at a schema that inherits from this one through allOf.
audit.rule.conversion-approximation.mess: collectionFormat: {construct} has no OpenAPI 3.0 equivalent here.
audit.rule.conversion-approximation.why: This document was converted from Swagger {from}, and 3.0 has no style for that delimiter (tsv nowhere, ssv/pipes/multi outside a query parameter). The value is serialized comma-separated instead, so what the try-it sends is not exactly what the document declares.
audit.rule.conversion-approximation.fix: Move the API's contract to a delimiter 3.x defines — csv, ssv, pipes or multi in a query parameter — and declare it with style and explode.
audit.rule.schema-dialect.label: Non-default JSON Schema dialect
audit.rule.schema-dialect.why: This documentation reads every schema as JSON Schema 2020-12, whatever the document declares. The keywords the two dialects share behave the same; the ones only your dialect has are read with 2020-12 meaning, or not at all.
audit.rule.schema-dialect.fix: If the schemas only use JSON Schema 2020-12 keywords, remove jsonSchemaDialect or point it at the OpenAPI base dialect; otherwise expect the keywords specific to your dialect not to be rendered.
audit.rule.unknown-field.label: Field the object does not have
audit.rule.unknown-field.message: “{field}” is not a field of the {object} Object in OpenAPI {declared}.
audit.rule.unknown-field.why: An OpenAPI object holds its own fields and x- extensions, nothing else. No tool reads this one — this documentation included — so whatever it was meant to say is silently lost; a misspelled description or required is the usual cause.
audit.rule.unknown-field.fix: Correct the name if it is a typo, prefix it with x- if it is your own data, or remove it.
audit.rule.required-field-missing.label: Required field missing
audit.rule.required-field-missing.messag: The {object} Object has no “{field}”, which OpenAPI requires.
audit.rule.required-field-missing.why: Validators reject the document, and code generators either stop or make a value up; this documentation shows what it can without it.
audit.rule.field-value-kind.label: Field with the wrong kind of value
audit.rule.field-value-kind.message: “{field}” of the {object} Object holds {value}, where OpenAPI expects {expected}.
audit.rule.field-value-kind.why: Validators reject it, and this documentation and most code generators read the field as absent: a parameter with no location, a security scheme with no type, a schema with no type.
audit.rule.field-value-kind.fix: Give {field} a value of the expected kind: {expected}.
audit.rule.parameter-schema-or-content.l: Parameter without exactly one schema or content
audit.rule.parameter-schema-or-content.m: This {object} needs either a schema or a content map with a single media type.
audit.rule.parameter-schema-or-content.w: With both, tools pick different ones; with neither, the value has no type at all — a bare text box in the try-it, an untyped argument in a generated client; with several media types, nothing says which one the value is sent as.
audit.rule.parameter-schema-or-content.f: Keep one: a schema (with style and explode for the serialization), or a content map holding exactly one media type with its schema.
audit.rule.exclusive-fields.label: Fields that exclude each other, both set
audit.rule.exclusive-fields.message: {first} and {second} are both set on this {object} Object, and only one of them may be.
audit.rule.exclusive-fields.why: The document says two things where one is allowed, and which one a tool keeps is not defined: this documentation and a generated client may each show a different one.
audit.rule.exclusive-fields.fix: Keep {first} or {second}, and remove the other.
audit.rule.header-object-fields.label: Header declaring a name or a location
audit.rule.header-object-fields.message: This header declares “{field}”, which a Header Object must not.
audit.rule.header-object-fields.why: A header is named by its key in the headers map and its location is implied, so the field is ignored — this documentation included. A name that differs from the key promises a header nobody will see.
audit.rule.header-object-fields.fix: Remove {field}; put the header's name as its key in the headers map.
audit.rule.component-key-format.label: Component name with characters OpenAPI does not allow
audit.rule.component-key-format.message: The component “{name}” in {section} uses characters a component name cannot hold.
audit.rule.component-key-format.why: Component names may only hold letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores. Validators reject the document, code generators that turn the name into a type or a file name fail or mangle it, and every $ref to it has to escape what it should not contain.
audit.rule.component-key-format.fix: Rename {name} with letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores only, and update every $ref that points to it.
audit.rule.status-code-valid.label: Response key that is not a status code
audit.rule.status-code-valid.message: “{status}” is not a status code, a range like 2XX, or default.
audit.rule.status-code-valid.why: A validator rejects it, a code generator matches no response to it, and this documentation shows the key as written, as if it were a status.
audit.rule.status-code-valid.fix: Use a three-digit status code from 100 to 599, a range with an uppercase X (4XX), or default.
audit.rule.media-type-key-syntax.label: Content key that is not a media type
audit.rule.media-type-key-syntax.why: This documentation sends the key as the request's Content-Type and reads the body's kind from it: a key it cannot read gives a body of unknown kind, sent with a Content-Type no server recognises. Code generators fare no better.
audit.rule.media-type-key-syntax.fix: Write a media type as type/subtype (application/json), a range (text/*, */*), with optional ; name=value parameters.
audit.rule.extension-reserved-prefix.mes: The extension “{field}” uses a prefix reserved for the OpenAPI Initiative.
audit.rule.extension-reserved-prefix.why: Extensions starting with x-oai- or x-oas- are reserved for uses the specification defines. Yours can collide with an official one later, and a tool that knows the official one will read your data as its own.
audit.rule.extension-reserved-prefix.fix: Rename it under a prefix of your own, such as x-acme-.
audit.rule.uri-form.label: Field that cannot be the URL or email it must be
audit.rule.uri-form.message: “{field}” of the {object} Object holds “{value}”, which is not a valid URL or email address.
audit.rule.uri-form.why: OpenAPI requires a URL, a URI or an email address here. Validators reject the document; this documentation leaves out a link it cannot parse, and other tools print a dead one.
audit.rule.uri-form.fix: Write a full URL (https://example.com/terms), a relative one, or an email address (api@example.com) — percent-encode spaces and special characters.
audit.rule.license-identifier-spdx.label: License identifier that is not an SPDX expression
audit.rule.license-identifier-spdx.messa: The license identifier “{identifier}” is not an SPDX license expression.
audit.rule.license-identifier-spdx.why: The identifier exists for machines: licence scanners, SBOM generators and registries match it against the SPDX list, and to them the API reads as unlicensed. This documentation shows the text as written.
audit.rule.license-identifier-spdx.fix: Use an identifier from spdx.org/licenses (MIT, Apache-2.0), an expression combining them (MIT OR Apache-2.0), or LicenseRef-YourName for a licence of your own; the name can stay human-readable.
audit.rule.self-uri.label: $self that is not a URI
audit.rule.self-uri.message: $self holds “{value}”, which is not a URI reference.
audit.rule.self-uri.why: $self is the document's own address and the base every relative $ref and server URL resolves against. Unable to read it, this documentation falls back to the URL the file was fetched from — exactly what $self was meant to override.
audit.rule.self-uri.fix: Write the document's URI (https://example.com/api/openapi.yaml), or remove $self.
audit.rule.tag-unique.label: Tag declared twice
audit.rule.tag-unique.message: The tag “{name}” is declared more than once.
audit.rule.tag-unique.why: Operations point at a tag by name, so both entries are one group: this documentation keeps the first declaration and drops the second — its description, its external docs, its place in the navigation.
audit.rule.tag-unique.fix: Merge the two entries for {name} into one.
audit.rule.tag-parent.label: Tag parent that does not exist or loops
audit.rule.tag-parent.message: The tag “{name}” names “{parent}” as its parent, which is not a declared tag or leads back to it.
audit.rule.tag-parent.why: The nesting cannot be built: this documentation files the tag at the top level of the navigation instead, and a tool that follows the chain of parents without a guard loops.
audit.rule.tag-parent.fix: Point parent at a tag declared in the tags list, and make sure no tag is, through its parents, its own ancestor.
audit.rule.path-syntax.label: Malformed path
audit.rule.path-syntax.message: “{path}” is not a valid path template.
audit.rule.path-syntax.why: A path starts with /, writes each variable once, its name in braces, and carries no query or fragment. Anything else cannot be appended to a server URL: a literal brace stays in the request, and after a # the query parameters never reach the server.
audit.rule.path-syntax.fix: Write {path} as a path: a leading /, each variable a name in balanced braces, used once, and query parameters declared as parameters rather than written into the path.
audit.rule.paths-identical.label: Identical paths
audit.rule.paths-identical.message: “{path}” is the same path as “{other}”, with other variable names.
audit.rule.paths-identical.why: Both describe the same URLs, which OpenAPI forbids: a server routes a request to one of them, and nothing says which. Here, a request pasted into the import dialog fits both, and the reader is asked to choose.
audit.rule.paths-identical.fix: Merge the operations of {path} into {other}, using one name for the variable.
audit.rule.paths-ambiguous.label: Ambiguous paths
audit.rule.paths-ambiguous.message: A URL can match both “{path}” and “{other}”.
audit.rule.paths-ambiguous.why: Each path is literal where the other has a variable, so matching concrete paths first cannot order them. OpenAPI leaves the choice to the tooling: servers, gateways and generated clients may each send the same request to a different operation, and the import dialog here asks the reader to choose.
audit.rule.paths-ambiguous.fix: Make one path literal wherever the other is, for instance by giving a fixed segment its own position in the URL.
audit.rule.parameters-unique.label: Parameter declared twice
audit.rule.parameters-unique.message: The {in} parameter “{name}” is declared twice in the same list.
audit.rule.parameters-unique.why: A parameter is one name in one location. Which declaration counts is left to whoever reads it: this documentation keeps the last one, a code generator may keep the first or emit two arguments with one name.
audit.rule.parameters-unique.fix: Keep one declaration of {name} in this list; to override a Path Item parameter, declare it on the operation instead.
audit.rule.header-parameter-ignored.mess: The header “{name}” is declared where OpenAPI says to ignore it.
audit.rule.header-parameter-ignored.why: Accept and Content-Type come from the media types, Authorization from the security schemes, a response's Content-Type from its content map, and a multipart part's from its encoding's contentType. Code generators drop such a declaration; this documentation shows such a parameter in the try-it and sends what is typed in it, over the body's own Content-Type and over the credential it injects.
audit.rule.header-parameter-ignored.fix: Remove the declaration: describe the formats with content or the encoding's contentType, the credential with a security scheme and a security requirement.
audit.rule.header-name-token.label: Invalid header name
audit.rule.header-name-token.message: “{name}” cannot be an HTTP header name.
audit.rule.header-name-token.why: A header name is a token: letters, digits and a few signs, with no space, colon or accented letter. No such header can exist on the wire — the browser refuses to send a request carrying it, and the try-it reports a failed send.
audit.rule.header-name-token.fix: Rename the header with letters, digits and hyphens only, such as X-Request-Id.
audit.rule.parameter-style-valid.label: Style not allowed here
audit.rule.parameter-style-valid.message: Style {style} does not apply to the {in} parameter “{name}”.
audit.rule.parameter-style-valid.why: Each style is defined for some locations and some types only — matrix and label in a path, deepObject for an object in a query. Outside them nothing says what goes on the wire: generators fall back to their own default, and the request built here uses a shape the server was never told to expect.
audit.rule.parameter-style-valid.fix: Pick a style defined for {in} parameters and for the parameter's type, or remove style to use the default.
audit.rule.querystring-parameter.label: Querystring parameter misused
audit.rule.querystring-parameter.message: The in: querystring parameter “{name}” cannot stand with “{conflict}”.
audit.rule.querystring-parameter.why: A querystring parameter is the whole query string as one value: it is described with content, never with schema, explode or allowReserved; an operation has at most one, and no in: query parameter sits beside it. Otherwise two declarations claim the same string, and the request built here matches neither.
audit.rule.querystring-parameter.fix: Describe {name} with content and a media type rather than schema, explode or allowReserved, keep a single querystring parameter, and fold any query parameters into its schema.
audit.rule.additional-operation-method.m: “{method}” cannot be a key of additionalOperations.
audit.rule.additional-operation-method.w: additionalOperations holds the methods the Path Item has no field for, spelled as sent. A method with its own field is ignored here — the operation written under it never appears — and a key that is not a method name makes the browser refuse every request built for it.
audit.rule.additional-operation-method.f: Move a standard method to its own field (post, get…); give any other one its exact name, without spaces.
audit.rule.server-variables.label: Server variable without a valid value
audit.rule.server-variables.message: The server URL {url} has no valid value for “{name}”.
audit.rule.server-variables.why: Every variable in braces in a server URL needs an entry whose default is one of its allowed values. Without one there is nothing to substitute: code generators reject the server, and the base URL here keeps the literal braces, so every request sent on it goes nowhere.
audit.rule.server-variables.fix: Declare {name} under the server's variables with a default, and list that default in its enum if it has one.
audit.rule.server-url-form.label: Server URL that is no URL template
audit.rule.server-url-form.message: The server URL “{url}” is not a valid URL template.
audit.rule.server-url-form.why: A server URL is a URL with variables in braces: no space, no character a URL cannot hold, no stray brace, and from OpenAPI 3.2 each variable used once. Otherwise there is nothing valid to send to: code generators reject the server, and the base URL here keeps the literal text, so every request sent on it goes nowhere.
audit.rule.server-url-form.fix: Write the URL as a URL — percent-encode or remove spaces and other characters a URL cannot hold, close every brace around a variable name — and use each variable once.
audit.rule.ref-siblings.label: Sibling of a $ref that tools ignore
audit.rule.ref-siblings.message: “{sibling}” sits next to a $ref to a {object} Object, and OpenAPI {declared} says to ignore it.
audit.rule.ref-siblings.why: This documentation lays the sibling over the referenced object, so it shows here; a validator or a code generator honouring the declared version drops it, and the two disagree on what the API says.
audit.rule.ref-siblings.fix: Move {sibling} into the referenced object, or wrap the reference (allOf: [ $ref ] next to the field in a schema); from OpenAPI 3.1, a summary or a description beside a $ref is kept.
audit.rule.ref-target-kind.label: $ref to the wrong kind of object
audit.rule.ref-target-kind.message: {ref} points to a {actual} Object where a {expected} Object belongs.
audit.rule.ref-target-kind.why: Whatever the pointer reaches is used in place: this documentation reads it as the wrong object — a parameter with no name, a header with a location — and validators reject the document.
audit.rule.ref-target-kind.fix: Point the $ref at a {expected} Object (components of the matching section), or declare one there.
audit.rule.ref-resolves.label: $ref that leads nowhere
audit.rule.ref-resolves.why: This documentation renders the rest of the document but shows nothing where the reference stands; validators and code generators stop on it.
audit.rule.ref-resolves.fix: Correct the pointer or the file name in {ref}, or declare what it should reach.
audit.rule.runtime-expression-syntax.mes: {expression} is not a runtime expression OpenAPI defines.
audit.rule.runtime-expression-syntax.why: Callbacks and links take values from a request or a response through these expressions; one that does not follow the grammar evaluates to nothing in any tool, and the reader has to guess what was meant.
audit.rule.runtime-expression-syntax.fix: Write it as $url, $method, $statusCode, or $request. / $response. followed by header.<name>, query.<name>, path.<name> or body#/<json-pointer>.
audit.rule.encoding-valid.label: Encoding entry the body never uses
audit.rule.encoding-valid.why: An encoding entry applies to a property of a form body — multipart or application/x-www-form-urlencoded, and before OpenAPI 3.2 a request body only. This one names no property, or sits on another body: no tool applies it, while this documentation still lists it under the media type.
audit.rule.encoding-valid.fix: Name a property the schema declares, move the encoding to the form body it was meant for, or remove it.
audit.rule.sequential-media.label: Stream field on a body that is not a stream
audit.rule.sequential-media.why: itemSchema describes one item of a sequential body (JSON Lines, server-sent events, multipart), and prefixEncoding and itemEncoding apply to multipart only, without an encoding map, and to an itemSchema or an array schema. Elsewhere tools ignore them, while this documentation shows a stream the API does not send.
audit.rule.sequential-media.fix: Use schema for a single-document body, keep the positional encodings for multipart with an itemSchema or an array schema, or change the media type to the stream the API sends.
audit.rule.responses-success.label: Operation with no success response
audit.rule.responses-success.message: This operation documents no 2XX or 3XX response, and no default.
audit.rule.responses-success.why: Code generators type a method's return value from its success response: with none, the method returns nothing and every call looks like an error. The reader sees only what goes wrong, and has to guess what a working call returns.
audit.rule.responses-success.fix: Add the response a successful call returns — 200, 201, 204… — with its content, or a default response.
audit.rule.discriminator-property.label: Discriminator on a property the payload may lack
audit.rule.discriminator-property.messag: The discriminator names “{property}”, which the schema does not declare as a required property.
audit.rule.discriminator-property.why: The discriminating property is what tells a client which variant it received. Undeclared, or optional with nothing to fall back on, it leaves a code generator's deserializer nothing to switch on — OpenAPI calls the behaviour undefined.
audit.rule.discriminator-property.fix: Declare {property} in the schema's properties (or in every variant's) and list it in required — or, from OpenAPI 3.2, give the discriminator a defaultMapping for payloads without it.
audit.rule.security-scopes.label: Scope the security scheme does not have
audit.rule.security-scopes.message: “{scope}” is required of “{name}”, whose {type} scheme declares no such scope.
audit.rule.security-scopes.why: An OAuth 2 client asks for the scopes a flow declares: the try-it preselects the operation's scopes among them, so it leaves this one out, and the token it fetches lacks what the call needs. In OpenAPI 3.0, a scheme other than oauth2 or openIdConnect takes no scopes at all.
audit.rule.security-scopes.fix: Declare {scope} in the scopes of the scheme's flows, correct its name, or remove it from the requirement.
audit.rule.enum-valid.label: Unusable enum
audit.rule.enum-valid.why: An empty enum admits no value at all; an entry the schema's own type rejects can never be sent; a duplicate becomes two constants of one name in a generated client, a compile error in Java or C#. This documentation offers every entry as written.
audit.rule.enum-valid.fix: Make enum a non-empty list of distinct values of the declared type, or correct the type.
audit.rule.nullable-enum-null.label: Nullable enum without null
audit.rule.nullable-enum-null.message: {declared} allows null, but the enum does not list it.
audit.rule.nullable-enum-null.why: Both keywords apply: the type admits null, then the enum rejects it, so null is never valid. Validators refuse it while generated clients send it, and a response carrying null fails its own schema.
audit.rule.nullable-enum-null.fix: Add null to the enum, or drop {declared} if the value can never be null.
audit.rule.array-items.label: Array without items
audit.rule.array-items.message: This array schema says nothing about its elements.
audit.rule.array-items.why: OpenAPI 3.0 requires items on an array. Without it this documentation shows array<any>, its sample is an empty list and the try-it has no editor for the elements; code generators type it as a list of anything.
audit.rule.array-items.fix: Add items with the schema of one element — a $ref to a component when the elements are objects.
audit.rule.constraint-type-mismatch.mess: {keyword} acts on none of the types this schema declares: it is ignored.
audit.rule.constraint-type-mismatch.why: JSON Schema applies each keyword to its own type only. No validator enforces this one and code generators drop it, while this documentation shows it as a constraint — a promise nobody keeps. The usual cause is a type changed after the constraint was written, or a constraint meant for items. OpenAPI 3.0's nullable is the same case with no type at all: it “only takes effect if type is explicitly defined within the same Schema Object” (3.0.4), so the composition beside it still rejects null, while this documentation shows the field as nullable.
audit.rule.constraint-type-mismatch.fix: Move {keyword} to the schema it was meant for (often items; for nullable, the schema the composition refers to), declare or correct the type, or remove it.
audit.rule.range-contradiction.label: Bounds no value satisfies
audit.rule.range-contradiction.why: Every value is rejected: the field can never be sent, and a response holding it is always invalid. A negative length or a multipleOf of zero is not even a valid schema.
audit.rule.range-contradiction.fix: Correct the bounds so that some value fits between them: the lower one at most the upper one, lengths and counts at least 0, multipleOf above 0.
audit.rule.pattern-valid.label: Pattern that is no regular expression
audit.rule.pattern-valid.message: /{pattern}/ is not a valid regular expression.
audit.rule.pattern-valid.why: JSON Schema expects an ECMA-262 regular expression. A validator compiling this one fails, often on the whole schema, and a generated client copies it into a check that throws at runtime; this documentation only shows it as written.
audit.rule.pattern-valid.fix: Fix the expression — close the group or bracket, escape the special character — and test it against a valid value.
audit.rule.format-valid.label: Format with no effect
audit.rule.format-valid.message: The format “{format}” has no effect on this schema; it would need {expected}.
audit.rule.format-valid.why: A format describes values of one type and is ignored on the others, and a misspelt one is unknown to every tool: validators skip it, and code generators fall back to the bare type — a date arrives as a plain string.
audit.rule.schema-keyword-typo.label: Misspelt schema keyword
audit.rule.schema-keyword-typo.why: JSON Schema ignores unknown keywords, so the constraint or annotation silently does nothing: no validator enforces it, no generator reads it, this documentation does not show it. required: true on a property is the draft-03 spelling; since draft-04 the property stays optional.
audit.rule.schema-keyword-typo.fix: Write {suggestion} — for required, in the required list of the object that holds the property.
audit.rule.composition-sanity.label: Composition that cannot mean what it says
audit.rule.composition-sanity.message: This {keyword} cannot mean what it says: {defect}.
audit.rule.composition-sanity.why: A choice of one is no choice: this documentation shows a “one of” over a single variant, and generators emit a union of one. A member listed twice in a oneOf makes every value matching it match twice, and oneOf accepts exactly one match — so no such value is ever valid. An allOf of disjoint types accepts nothing at all.
audit.rule.composition-sanity.fix: Write the single member in place of the {keyword}, list each member once, or give the allOf members types that can hold together.
audit.rule.readonly-writeonly.label: Property both read-only and write-only
audit.rule.readonly-writeonly.message: This schema is marked both readOnly and writeOnly.
audit.rule.readonly-writeonly.why: The value may never be sent and is never returned, so it exists nowhere: this documentation leaves it out of request and response samples alike, and generators have to pick which flag to believe. OpenAPI 3.0 forbids the pair outright.
audit.rule.readonly-writeonly.fix: Keep the one that is true: readOnly for a value the server sets, writeOnly for one the client sends and never gets back (a password).
audit.rule.recursion-unsatisfiable.label: Schema that requires itself
audit.rule.recursion-unsatisfiable.messa: The required property “{property}” leads back to this schema, with nothing to end the chain.
audit.rule.recursion-unsatisfiable.why: A valid value would have to contain itself forever: no finite payload satisfies the schema. Validators reject every one, generators produce a type whose constructor needs an instance of itself, and this documentation's sample stops at its depth limit with a value the API would refuse.
audit.rule.recursion-unsatisfiable.fix: Give the chain an end: make {property} optional, allow null, or turn it into an array that may be empty.
audit.rule.merge-patch-required.label: Merge patch with required properties
audit.rule.merge-patch-required.why: A JSON Merge Patch carries only the members that change, and any of them may be left out. A required list says the opposite: clients built from it must send the whole resource on every update, and the try-it marks every field mandatory. Usually the resource's own schema, reused for its patch.
audit.rule.merge-patch-required.fix: Give the patch a schema of its own without required, or drop required from the reused one where it serves as a patch.
audit.rule.multipart-schema-object.label: Form body with no fields
audit.rule.multipart-schema-object.messa: This {mediaType} body has no object schema with properties to make fields from.
audit.rule.multipart-schema-object.why: A form is a set of named fields, and the schema's top-level properties are their names. The try-it builds one field per property: with none to read, the body section stays empty and the request leaves without a body. Generators have nothing to name the parts after either.
audit.rule.multipart-schema-object.fix: Describe the body as type: object, with one property per form field — a string with format: binary for a file.
audit.rule.binary-placement.label: Raw bytes where only text can go
audit.rule.binary-placement.message: This schema declares raw bytes inside {container}, which only carries text.
audit.rule.binary-placement.why: JSON, a URL and a header are text: a file cannot travel there as it is. Generators type the field as a byte stream they cannot serialize, and this documentation prefills an empty string where the file would go — or, for a whole JSON body declared binary, sends the picked file labelled as JSON.
audit.rule.binary-placement.fix: Carry the bytes as base64 text (format: byte, or contentEncoding: base64), or send the file as its own body or as a multipart part.
audit.rule.example-has-ref.label: Example that is only a $ref
audit.rule.example-has-ref.message: This example's value is just {ref}, a $ref written as data.
audit.rule.example-has-ref.why: An example is data, and a $ref inside data is data too: this documentation shows the literal object, and the try-it prefills it as the body to send. A reference to a shared example belongs on the Example Object itself, not in its value.
audit.rule.example-has-ref.fix: Move the $ref up one level, as an entry of the examples map: examples: { name: { $ref: {ref} } }.
audit.rule.problem-status-mismatch.label: Problem details with another status
audit.rule.problem-status-mismatch.messa: This problem+json response is documented under {status}, but its status says {value}.
audit.rule.problem-status-mismatch.why: In problem details (RFC 9457), status is the code the server generated for this very occurrence. A client that reads it — many log it, some prefer it to the status line — is told something the response contradicts. Usually an example copied from a neighbouring response.
audit.rule.problem-status-mismatch.fix: Set status to {status} in the example or the schema, or document the problem under the code it carries.
audit.rule.request-body-method.label: Request body on a method that gives it no meaning
audit.rule.request-body-method.message: A request body on {method}: RFC 9110 gives content no meaning with GET, HEAD or DELETE and forbids it with TRACE. With GET or HEAD, the try-it sends the request without it.
audit.rule.request-body-method.why: RFC 9110 says content in a GET, HEAD or DELETE request has no defined semantics and may get the request rejected as a smuggling attempt (§9.3.1, §9.3.2, §9.3.5): a client should not send it unless the server said it supports it. A TRACE request must not carry any (§9.3.8). OpenAPI 3.0 tells tools to ignore such a request body; 3.1 and 3.2 allow it and say to avoid it. Browsers refuse a body with GET or HEAD, so this documentation's try-it sends those requests without it, says so, and keeps the body in the cURL command; a DELETE body it sends as written. A GET or HEAD body is a warning, a DELETE body a note — some APIs read one on purpose — and a TRACE body an error.
audit.rule.request-body-method.fix: Move what the {method} body carries into query parameters, or use POST — or QUERY, the HTTP method made for a query sent as content. A DELETE body the server really reads can stay: say so in the description.
audit.rule.bodyless-status.label: Content on a response that carries none
audit.rule.bodyless-status.message: This {status} response declares content, which RFC 9110 rules out for a 1xx, 204, 205 or 304 response and for any response to HEAD.
audit.rule.bodyless-status.why: RFC 9110: 1xx, 204 and 304 responses never include content (§6.4.1), a server must not generate content in a 205 (§15.3.6), and must not send content in any response to HEAD (§9.3.2). The schema describes a body no client ever receives: a generated client types the call's result from it and parses an empty stream, and this documentation shows that body and its sample under the status as if it came.
audit.rule.bodyless-status.fix: Remove the content map from the {status} response. For HEAD, declare the headers the GET would send and no content; if the response is shared with the GET, give the HEAD operation its own.
audit.rule.http-date-headers.label: Date header not declared as an HTTP date
audit.rule.http-date-headers.message: The HTTP RFCs make {header} an HTTP date, like Sun, 06 Nov 1994 08:49:37 GMT (Retry-After may also be a number of seconds); this declaration describes another format.
audit.rule.http-date-headers.why: Retry-After and Last-Modified (RFC 9110), Expires (RFC 9111) and Sunset (RFC 8594) carry an HTTP date, which a sender must write in the IMF-fixdate form: Sun, 06 Nov 1994 08:49:37 GMT (RFC 9110 §5.6.7). format: date-time or date describes RFC 3339 (1994-11-06T08:49:37Z), which HTTP date parsers are not required to read, and a number is no date at all — RFC 9111 tells caches to treat Expires: 0 as an invalid date. A client generated from the declaration fails to parse every real response. Only Retry-After may carry a delay instead: a non-negative integer of seconds.
audit.rule.http-date-headers.fix: Declare {header} as type: string, format: http-date (OpenAPI Format Registry), with an example like Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT. A Retry-After given in seconds can stay an integer.
audit.rule.query-method-body.label: QUERY operation without request content
audit.rule.query-method-body.message: This QUERY operation declares no request body with a media type, and RFC 10008 makes a server refuse a QUERY request without a Content-Type.
audit.rule.query-method-body.why: QUERY (RFC 10008, the method OpenAPI 3.2's query field defines) is a safe, repeatable request whose content and its media type define the query (§2); servers must fail the request when the Content-Type is missing or does not match the content. Declared without a request body or without content, the operation describes a request every conforming server refuses: a generated client sends it empty, and this documentation's try-it has no body to edit.
audit.rule.query-method-body.fix: Declare the request body with the media type of the query: application/json with its schema, or a query language's own type. If the operation takes no content, make it a GET with query parameters.
audit.rule.problem-details-shape.label: Problem details schema against RFC 9457
audit.rule.problem-details-shape.message: This application/problem+json schema contradicts RFC 9457 at {member}: problem details are a JSON object whose type, title, detail and instance are strings and whose status is a number.
audit.rule.problem-details-shape.why: RFC 9457 makes problem details a JSON object (§3) whose standard members have fixed types: type and instance a string holding a URI reference, title and detail strings, status a number (§3.1). A client must ignore a member of the wrong type — a status declared as a string is dropped by every conforming reader — and a client generated from the schema expects what no problem-aware library hands over. A root that is not an object is not problem details at all. $ names the root, $.status a member.
audit.rule.problem-details-shape.fix: Make the schema an object and give the standard members their RFC types: status an integer, type and instance strings (format: uri-reference), title and detail strings. Put API-specific data in extension members, and use application/json for an error body that is not problem details.
audit.rule.operation-described.label: Operation with neither summary nor description
audit.rule.operation-described.message: This operation has neither summary nor description.
audit.rule.operation-described.why: It shows up as a bare method and path, in the page as in the navigation: the reader has to guess what it does from its URL.
audit.rule.operation-described.fix: Add a summary — a short phrase starting with a verb, shown in the navigation — and a description saying when to use the operation and what it changes.
audit.rule.parameter-described.label: Parameter without description
audit.rule.parameter-described.why: The try-it labels the field with the parameter name and explains it with this description. Without one, the reader gets a box to fill and no idea what belongs in it.
audit.rule.parameter-described.fix: Add a description saying what the value means, its unit or format, and what happens when it is omitted.
audit.rule.request-body-described.label: Request body without description
audit.rule.request-body-described.messag: The request body has no description.
audit.rule.request-body-described.why: The schema says which fields exist, never which ones go together, what a partial update accepts, or what the API does with them.
audit.rule.request-body-described.fix: Add a description to the requestBody: what the payload represents, which fields go together, and what a partial update accepts.
audit.rule.property-described.label: Schema with undescribed properties
audit.rule.property-described.message: Properties of this schema with no description ({count}): {names}.
audit.rule.property-described.why: The schema view and the body editor show this description next to the field; without one the reader gets a name and a type, and infers the rest.
audit.rule.property-described.fix: Add a description to each of these properties saying what the field means, its unit or format, and when it can be absent or null — a title that only repeats the name does not count.
audit.rule.error-responses-documented.la: Mutating operation with no error response
audit.rule.error-responses-documented.me: This mutating operation documents no error response.
audit.rule.error-responses-documented.wh: Only the happy path is described, while validation, conflict and permission errors are exactly where a consumer needs help.
audit.rule.error-responses-documented.fi: Document the 4xx responses the operation can return (400, 404, 409, 422…) with their error body, or at least a default response.
audit.rule.response-example.label: Success response with no example
audit.rule.response-example.message: The {status} response’s payload has no example, or only placeholders.
audit.rule.response-example.why: The app then shows a sample generated from the schema — structurally right, semantically empty. A placeholder example such as "string" shows no more than that sample. A hand-written example shows what a real payload looks like.
audit.rule.response-example.fix: Add an example with realistic values the API really returns — on the shared schema when the payload is one, else on the response’s media type.
audit.rule.info-described.label: info.description missing
audit.rule.info-described.why: It is this documentation's home page: without it the reader lands on a title and a list of endpoints, with nothing about what the API is for or how to get access to it.
audit.rule.info-described.fix: Write info.description: what the API is for, how to get access and credentials, and where to start.
audit.rule.info-metadata.label: info field missing or unusable
audit.rule.info-metadata.message: info.{field} is missing, or gives the reader nothing to act on.
audit.rule.info-metadata.why: Who to ask when the API misbehaves, and under what terms it may be used: two fields filled once for the life of the document, and the reader has no other way to find the answers. A contact counts with an email or a URL — a name alone reaches no one. A licence counts with an SPDX identifier, a URL to its text, or a name that is itself an SPDX expression, such as MIT or Apache-2.0.
audit.rule.info-metadata.fix: Give info.contact an email or a URL, and info.license an SPDX identifier, a URL to its text, or an SPDX name.
audit.rule.response-content-schema.label: Response content with no schema
audit.rule.response-content-schema.messa: The {mediaType} content of response {status} has no schema.
audit.rule.response-content-schema.why: The media type names a format and nothing of the payload: a generated client gets no type for it, and this documentation shows the body as any, with null as its generated example (none at all for XML). JSON, XML and forms have a structure only a schema describes; a file or plain text is its own description.
audit.rule.response-content-schema.fix: Add the schema of the payload under {mediaType}, a $ref to a component when it is shared. For a stream of items (OpenAPI 3.2), add an itemSchema.
audit.rule.example-placeholder.label: Placeholder example
audit.rule.example-placeholder.message: The example {value} is a placeholder, not a value.
audit.rule.example-placeholder.why: Readers take an example as the API's own word for what a real payload looks like, and the try-it prefills it as the value to send. A JSON type name, TODO or lorem ipsum — Swagger's generated {"id": 0, "name": "string"} — fills the slot and shows nothing, so the example rules do not count it as an example. A value the schema's enum or const allows is never a placeholder.
audit.rule.example-placeholder.fix: Replace it with a realistic value the API really accepts or returns, or remove it: the sample this documentation generates says as much.
audit.rule.placeholder-text.label: Placeholder in a display label
audit.rule.placeholder-text.message: {field} holds “{value}”, a placeholder, and it is shown as the name.
audit.rule.placeholder-text.why: These fields are display text and nothing else: the title heads every page and the browser tab, a summary names the API, a tag group or a response wherever it appears. A placeholder there (TODO, Title, string, lorem ipsum) is printed as that name, and tells the reader the document was never finished.
audit.rule.placeholder-text.fix: Replace {field} with the real name: a few words the reader recognizes.
audit.rule.tag-described.label: Tag without description
audit.rule.tag-described.message: The tag “{name}” has no description saying what its group covers.
audit.rule.tag-described.why: A tag is a chapter of the documentation, and its description is the chapter's introduction: other renderers print it at the head of the group, this documentation shows it as the navigation group's tooltip. Without it, the reader learns what the group covers by opening its operations one by one. A description that reads the tag's name back, or a placeholder, counts as none.
audit.rule.tag-described.fix: Give “{name}” a description in the top-level tags list: what the group covers, and how its operations fit together.
audit.rule.redirect-location.label: Redirect without a Location header
audit.rule.redirect-location.message: This {status} redirect documents no Location header: a client cannot tell where it is sent.
audit.rule.redirect-location.why: RFC 9110 says the server should send a Location header with the new URI in a 301 and a 308, and with the other URI in a 302 and a 307 (§15.4); a 303 is defined by the URI its Location header carries. Without it in the document, a client author learns that the answer is elsewhere and nothing about how to follow it, and neither does an agent reading the operation.
audit.rule.redirect-location.fix: Declare a Location header on the {status} response (type: string, format: uri-reference), with an example of the URI it carries. If several operations share the response, declare it once under components.responses.
audit.rule.method-not-allowed-allow.mess: This {status} response documents no Allow header, which RFC 9110 requires the server to send.
audit.rule.method-not-allowed-allow.why: RFC 9110 §15.5.6: the origin server must send an Allow header in a 405, listing the methods the resource supports. A client told “not this method” learns from it which ones are — if the document tells its author the header is there to read.
audit.rule.method-not-allowed-allow.fix: Declare an Allow header on the 405 response (type: string, example: GET, HEAD). If several operations share the response, declare it once under components.responses.
audit.rule.partial-content-range.label: 206 response without Content-Range
audit.rule.partial-content-range.message: This {status} response documents neither a Content-Range header nor a multipart/byteranges body, and RFC 9110 requires one of them.
audit.rule.partial-content-range.why: RFC 9110 §15.3.7: a 206 holding one range must carry a Content-Range header saying which bytes it holds; one holding several must be multipart/byteranges, each part with its own Content-Range. A client resuming a download or reading a slice needs one or the other to place the bytes it got.
audit.rule.partial-content-range.fix: Declare a Content-Range header on the response (type: string, example: bytes 0-1023/146515), or a multipart/byteranges media type if the server returns several ranges at once.
audit.rule.link-target.label: Link pointing nowhere
audit.rule.link-target.message: The link {link} points at {target}, which this document declares nowhere.
audit.rule.link-target.why: A link is the API telling the reader which call comes next. Pointing it at an operation the document does not declare breaks the chain it advertises, and the documentation shows the link with nothing to follow.
audit.rule.link-target.fix: Name an operationId this document declares, or set operationRef to a JSON pointer to one of its operations.
audit.rule.deprecation-replacement.label: Deprecation naming no replacement
audit.rule.deprecation-replacement.messa: This deprecation names no replacement and no sunset.
audit.rule.deprecation-replacement.why: The reader learns the thing is going away, not what to do about it.
audit.rule.deprecation-replacement.fix: Name the successor in the description (“Use … instead”), or give the sunset date.
audit.rule.deprecation-header-format.lab: Deprecation header with the wrong value type
audit.rule.deprecation-header-format.mes: This Deprecation header declares {declared}, where RFC 9745 requires a Structured Field Date: @ and seconds since 1970, such as @1688169599.
audit.rule.deprecation-header-format.why: RFC 9745 (§2.1) says the Deprecation field's value MUST be a Date as defined by RFC 9651 (§3.3.7): @ followed by an integer number of seconds. The early drafts took true or an HTTP-date, and documents still say so. A client written from this document parses a value the API, once it follows the RFC, never sends — and a client that reads the header to warn its developers stays silent. This documentation prints the declared type next to the header's name, so the reader takes the wrong shape from the page too.
audit.rule.deprecation-header-format.fix: Declare the header as type: string with an example such as @1688169599, and give the date in words in the description. Announce the removal date in a Sunset header.
audit.rule.sunset-before-deprecation.mes: The examples set the Sunset ({sunset}) before the Deprecation ({deprecation}). RFC 9745 forbids a Sunset date earlier than the Deprecation date.
audit.rule.sunset-before-deprecation.why: RFC 9745 (§4): "The timestamp given in the Sunset HTTP header field MUST NOT be earlier than the one given in the Deprecation header field." The two examples describe a timeline no server may send — the removal before the warning — and a client written from them learns it. Only examples that parse are compared: a Deprecation of the form @seconds, a Sunset in the HTTP date format (Sun, 06 Nov 1994 08:49:37 GMT).
audit.rule.sunset-before-deprecation.fix: Correct whichever example is wrong, so that the Sunset ({sunset}) comes at or after the Deprecation ({deprecation}).
audit.rule.deprecated-but-required.label: Deprecated input still required
audit.rule.deprecated-but-required.messa: “{name}” is deprecated and still required: clients are told to stop sending what the API refuses to go without.
audit.rule.deprecated-but-required.why: OpenAPI says a deprecated parameter SHOULD be transitioned out of usage, and JSON Schema 2020-12 (§9.3) that applications SHOULD refrain from using a deprecated property. Required says the request is rejected without it. A client that follows the deprecation breaks its own calls; one that keeps sending it is told it is doing wrong. One of the two flags is stale. A response property is not concerned: the server keeps sending it until removal.
audit.rule.deprecated-but-required.fix: Make “{name}” optional while it is deprecated — the server falling back on its replacement or a default — or drop the deprecated flag if clients must still send it.
audit.rule.parameter-naming.label: Parameter off the dominant convention
audit.rule.parameter-naming.message: The parameter “{name}” is {style} where the document is mostly {dominant}.
audit.rule.parameter-naming.why: Consumers type these names by hand: a document that mixes conventions turns each of them into a coin flip.
audit.rule.parameter-naming.fix: Rename the parameter to the document's dominant convention in the API's next version, or accept the mix knowingly — a rename breaks existing clients.
audit.rule.property-naming.label: Property off the dominant convention
audit.rule.property-naming.message: The property “{name}” is {style} where the document is mostly {dominant}.
audit.rule.property-naming.why: A payload whose keys change convention from one endpoint to the next forces a mapping layer on every consumer — and that layer gets it wrong once.
audit.rule.property-naming.fix: Rename the property to the dominant convention in the API's next version, or accept the exception knowingly — a rename breaks existing clients.
audit.rule.path-style.label: Path segment off the dominant convention
audit.rule.path-style.message: The segment “{segment}” is {style} where the paths are mostly {dominant}.
audit.rule.path-style.why: URLs are the most public and the least renameable surface of an API: they end up in logs, in bookmarks and in other people's code. A mixed convention costs a lookup on every call.
audit.rule.path-style.fix: Rename the segment to the paths' dominant convention in the API's next version, keeping the old path as an alias until clients have moved.
audit.rule.operation-id-collision.label: operationIds generating one name
audit.rule.operation-id-collision.messag: operationIds “{operationId}” and “{other}” become one name once camelized: generated SDKs give both one method name.
audit.rule.operation-id-collision.why: Code generators turn an operationId into a method name: openapi-generator camelizes it (get_user → getUser), and when two operations of one tag land on the same name it renames the later one getUser_0, with a warning. Which operation keeps the plain name then depends on declaration order, and moving one in the document renames the other's method in every SDK built from the next version.
audit.rule.operation-id-collision.fix: Rename “{operationId}” or “{other}” so that the two stay distinct once camelized (separators dropped, the first letter and each letter after a separator in either case): a verb and a noun that say what each one does.
audit.rule.property-name-collision.label: Properties generating one field
audit.rule.property-name-collision.messa: The properties “{name}” and “{other}” of the same schema become one name once camelized: generated models give both one field name.
audit.rule.property-name-collision.why: openapi-generator camelizes property names (user_id → userId) but tells properties apart by their JSON name, so user_id and userId both generate a userId field and a getUserId() method — a Java model that does not compile (openapi-generator issues #8291 and #20484, answered with a per-name mapping option every consumer has to set). The JSON is valid; the SDK built from it is not.
audit.rule.property-name-collision.fix: Keep one of “{name}” and “{other}”, or rename one so that the two stay distinct once camelized: separators dropped, the first letter and each letter after a separator in either case.
audit.rule.schema-name-collision.label: Schema names generating one type
audit.rule.schema-name-collision.message: The schema “{name}” differs from “{other}” only by case or separators: generated SDKs give both one type name.
audit.rule.schema-name-collision.why: openapi-generator turns ., -, :, space, | and / in a schema name into _ and camelizes the result: Pet.Status, pet_status and PetStatus all generate one PetStatus class. One file is written, the last schema silently overwriting the others, with no warning — every operation typed with a lost schema then returns another one's shape. Names differing by case alone stay two classes, in two files that a case-insensitive file system (macOS, Windows) holds as one.
audit.rule.schema-name-collision.fix: Rename “{name}” or “{other}” so that the two differ by more than case and separators.
audit.rule.operation-id-present.label: Operation without operationId
audit.rule.operation-id-present.message: No operationId — the deep link falls back to “{fallbackId}”.
audit.rule.operation-id-present.why: That fallback is derived from the method and the path, so every link a reader shares breaks the day the path is renamed.
audit.rule.operation-id-present.fix: Give the operation a stable, unique operationId — a verb and a noun, in letters, digits and underscores (listPets).
audit.rule.operation-tagged.label: Operation without tag
audit.rule.operation-tagged.why: It lands in the navigation's catch-all group along with every other untagged operation, and the reader cannot tell which family it belongs to.
audit.rule.operation-tagged.fix: Add at least one tag, and declare it with a description in the top-level tags list.
audit.rule.servers-declared.label: No server declared
audit.rule.servers-declared.why: Environment seeding has nothing to offer: the reader has to type a base URL by hand before the first try-it call.
audit.rule.servers-declared.fix: Declare one servers entry per environment, each with a url and a description (Production, Sandbox).
audit.rule.security-scheme-described.why: The credentials block shows that description to explain what to paste and where to get it. Without one, the reader faces a bare field labelled with the scheme's key.
audit.rule.security-scheme-described.fix: Add a description to the scheme saying where to get the credential and in what form to paste it.
audit.rule.oauth-flow-urls.label: OAuth flow missing a URL
audit.rule.oauth-flow-urls.why: The try-it runs this flow itself and cannot without that URL: the reader falls back to pasting a token by hand.
audit.rule.oauth-flow-urls.fix: Add the missing URL to the flow: authorizationUrl for authorization code and implicit flows, tokenUrl for authorization code, password and client credentials flows.
audit.rule.operation-summary-present.mes: This operation has a description but no summary, so it is shown as “{label}”.
audit.rule.operation-summary-present.why: This documentation names an operation by its summary — in the navigation and as the page heading — and falls back to its path, or a webhook's name; the tab title becomes the method and path, the pager link a bare “Next”. Without summaries the navigation reads as a list of URLs, while the sentence that would name each operation sits in its description. A placeholder summary is shown as the name just the same.
audit.rule.operation-summary-present.fix: Add a summary: a short phrase starting with a verb (“List pets”), drawn from the first sentence of the description.
audit.rule.operation-summary-style.label: Markup in a summary
audit.rule.operation-summary-style.messa: The summary contains {markup}, which is printed as typed: a summary is plain text.
audit.rule.operation-summary-style.why: Unlike the description, OpenAPI's summary is plain text, and this documentation shows it as such everywhere: the navigation, the page heading, the tab title, a callback's line, the pager. Asterisks, backticks, brackets and tags appear as typed, and a line break is collapsed where the summary is shown on one line.
audit.rule.operation-summary-style.fix: Write the summary as one line of plain text, and keep the formatting for the description.
audit.rule.tag-declared.label: Undeclared tag
audit.rule.tag-declared.message: Operations carry the tag “{name}”, which the top-level tags list does not declare.
audit.rule.tag-declared.why: It still makes a navigation group, but one with nothing to say: no description, no external docs, and no place of its own in the order — undeclared groups come after every declared one, in the order operations first use them. The tags list is where the reading order and each group's introduction are written.
audit.rule.tag-declared.fix: Declare “{name}” in the top-level tags list, with a description, at its place in the reading order.
audit.rule.tag-unused.label: Declared tag nothing carries
audit.rule.tag-unused.message: No operation carries the declared tag “{name}”, so this documentation hides it.
audit.rule.tag-unused.why: The navigation is built from the tags operations carry: a tag no operation, webhook or callback carries, and that is no parent of a carried tag, is hidden, its description and external docs with it. It is usually left over from a removed endpoint, or spelled differently from the name the operations use.
audit.rule.tag-unused.fix: Remove “{name}” from the tags list, or tag the operations it was meant for with exactly that name.
audit.rule.markdown-unsafe.label: HTML the sanitizer removes
audit.rule.markdown-unsafe.message: {construct} in this description is removed when the Markdown is rendered: readers never see it.
audit.rule.markdown-unsafe.why: A renderer that turns Markdown into a page has to strip what could run code or take over the page, and OpenAPI lets it ignore those features. This documentation passes every description it renders through DOMPurify's HTML profile, with style and form controls removed too: scripts, frames, embeds, SVG, MathML, unknown elements, on* event attributes and other attributes outside the allow-list are dropped, and so are links whose scheme is not http, https, mailto, tel or a few others (data: only on images). An accidental tag such as List<Pet> or /users/<id> is read as an element, and disappears as well.
audit.rule.markdown-unsafe.fix: Remove {construct}, or put it between backticks if it is meant to be read as text. For a video or a diagram, link to it with an https URL.
audit.rule.markdown-links.label: Relative link in a description
audit.rule.markdown-links.message: The link to {target} is relative: it resolves against the page showing the description, not against the document.
audit.rule.markdown-links.why: OpenAPI says relative references in CommonMark hyperlinks are resolved in their rendered context, which might differ from the context of the API description (OAS 3.2 §4.1.2.2.3). This documentation sets no base URL and rewrites no link: the target resolves against the documentation page's own address, so the image does not load and the link lands on a page of the documentation host that does not exist. A #fragment link is fine: here it scrolls to that anchor.
audit.rule.markdown-links.fix: Write {target} as an absolute https URL.
audit.rule.document-has-operations.label: Nothing to document
audit.rule.document-has-operations.messa: This document declares no operation and no webhook: there is nothing to document.
audit.rule.document-has-operations.why: This documentation opens on a home page saying the schema declares no operations, above an empty navigation; a code generator produces a client with no method. OpenAPI 3.1 allows a document made of components only, a library other documents reference: such a document is not one to publish as an API reference.
audit.rule.document-has-operations.fix: Add the API's paths, or publish the document that references these components instead. For a components library, switch this rule off.
audit.rule.example-external-only.label: Example only in an external file
audit.rule.example-external-only.message: This example's only value is in another file, which this documentation does not fetch.
audit.rule.example-external-only.why: A page that fetches whatever URL a document names is a request-forgery tool, so this documentation shows an externalValue as a link, and neither the try-it nor the response example can use it. Any other renderer needs the host to allow cross-origin requests, and in OpenAPI 3.0 a relative URL resolves against a base each tool picks for itself.
audit.rule.example-external-only.fix: In OpenAPI 3.2, add the value inline as dataValue beside externalValue. Before 3.2 the two are mutually exclusive: write the value inline as value instead of the link.
audit.rule.type-missing.label: Value with no type
audit.rule.type-missing.message: This schema says nothing about the value it describes.
audit.rule.type-missing.why: No type, no values, no structure: the reader learns that the field exists and nothing of its kind, and a generated client gets no type for it. This documentation shows it as any, and its generated example holds null in its place. This rule grades what the API sends — response bodies, and the requests of webhooks and callbacks; what an agent fills in is untyped-input's.
audit.rule.type-missing.fix: Give it a type, with a format, an enum or properties where they apply. In OpenAPI 3.0, nullable: true has no effect without a type next to it.
audit.rule.forbidden-in-browser.label: Header or method a browser refuses
audit.rule.forbidden-in-browser.message: Browsers refuse to send “{name}” from a page: the try-it cannot send it, and no browser client can.
audit.rule.forbidden-in-browser.why: The Fetch standard forbids a page's script to set some headers — Host, Cookie, Origin, Content-Length, any Sec- or Proxy- name, a method override carrying TRACE — and to use the CONNECT, TRACE and TRACK methods. The browser drops such a header without a word and refuses such a method. This documentation's try-it names the headers it will not send and blocks the method, pointing at the cURL command instead.
audit.rule.forbidden-in-browser.fix: Leave out the headers the browser sets itself (Host, Origin, Content-Length…). When a header or a method is for server-side clients only, say so in the description.
audit.rule.server-placeholder.label: Server left at an example host
audit.rule.server-placeholder.message: {url} is a host reserved for documentation examples: requests sent there never reach the API.
audit.rule.server-placeholder.why: RFC 2606 reserves example.com, example.net, example.org and the .example and .invalid domains so that documentation never points at a real host. The try-it sends to this server — the operation's own, else the environment seeded from a root server or the first root server — and the reader gets a network error. Names under .test and localhost are not flagged: they are set aside for testing and local servers.
audit.rule.server-placeholder.fix: Write the API's real base URL. When each reader has their own host, put the part that varies in a server variable, with a default and a description.
audit.rule.server-described.label: Server known only by its URL
audit.rule.server-described.message: The server {url} has no description to tell it from the others.
audit.rule.server-described.why: With several servers, the reader picks one by its label. This documentation names the environment seeded from a server after its name (OpenAPI 3.2), else its description, else its URL — a list of URLs the reader has to decode before every call. A placeholder description such as TODO says nothing either.
audit.rule.server-described.fix: Add a description saying what this server is (Production, EU sandbox), or, in OpenAPI 3.2, a name.
audit.rule.untyped-input.label: Input with no type
audit.rule.untyped-input.message: This input's schema says nothing about its value.
audit.rule.untyped-input.why: Tools built from this operation copy the schema as it is: the agent gets a field with no type and guesses, and a string where the API wants a number is a failed call. This documentation shows it as any, offers a plain text box, sends what is typed as text — 42 leaves a JSON body as "42" — and has no sample to generate for it.
audit.rule.untyped-input.fix: Give it a type, with a format, an enum or bounds where they apply. For a JSON body declared without a schema, add the schema of the payload.
audit.rule.free-form-input.label: Input object with no shape
audit.rule.free-form-input.message: This input object declares no properties and accepts any key.
audit.rule.free-form-input.why: An agent filling it in has every key to invent and nothing to check them against: tools copy the schema as it is. OpenAI's strict mode refuses it outright — it requires declared properties and additionalProperties: false.
audit.rule.free-form-input.fix: Declare the properties the API reads and close the object with additionalProperties: false. If the keys really are data, type the values instead: additionalProperties: { type: string }.
audit.rule.union-ambiguous.label: Union branches an agent cannot tell apart
audit.rule.union-ambiguous.message: Branches {keyword}/{first} and {keyword}/{second} both take {type} values, and nothing says which one to send.
audit.rule.union-ambiguous.why: Tools carry the union inlined, component names gone: the agent sees two nameless shapes of one type and picks one, and a payload matching the wrong branch is rejected. OpenAI's strict mode and Gemini do not support oneOf at all.
audit.rule.union-ambiguous.fix: Give each branch a title and a description saying when to send it, or add a discriminator.
audit.rule.input-root-shape.label: Request body that is not an object
audit.rule.input-root-shape.message: The root of this {mediaType} body is {shape}, where a tool expects an object.
audit.rule.input-root-shape.why: A tool's input is an object of named arguments. GPT Actions skips the operation; @ivotoby/openapi-mcp-server, one of the bridges of this documentation's MCP export, wraps an array or a scalar under a body property the document never named and makes a union the tool's root; Anthropic's API and OpenAI's strict mode require an object root and refuse a union.
audit.rule.input-root-shape.fix: When the API can change, wrap the payload in an object — { "items": [...] } rather than a bare array, one object with optional members rather than a oneOf. Otherwise accept the finding knowingly in the audit configuration.
audit.rule.enum-values-undescribed.label: Enum values with no meaning attached
audit.rule.enum-values-undescribed.messa: This enum offers {count} values, and nothing explains these: {missing}.
audit.rule.enum-values-undescribed.why: A tool built from the operation carries the values and what the schema says about them, nothing more: offered S, M and XL, or 1, 2 and 3, an agent guesses which one the user's request means. A description naming each value travels to every tool. The x-enum-descriptions extension is shown by this documentation, value by value, and by Redocly, but OpenAI strict mode keeps standard keywords only and drops it.
audit.rule.enum-values-undescribed.fix: Say what {missing} mean in the schema's description ("asc: oldest first; desc: newest first"), and add x-enum-descriptions for the list of values this documentation shows.
audit.rule.parameter-name-collision.mess: “{name}” is both a {first} input and a {second} input of this operation.
audit.rule.parameter-name-collision.why: HTTP tells the two apart by location; a tool has one flat list of argument names. Both OpenAPI-to-MCP bridges key parameters by name, so the last one silently overwrites the other, and one of them renames a clashing body property body_{name}, a name the document never gives. Semantic Kernel's OpenAPI plugin refuses the clash, case aside, and leaves the whole operation out — logged, with no error to the caller.
