audit.rule.parameter-name-collision.fix: Rename one of the two inputs so that every input of the operation has a name of its own, case aside — the body's {name} usually has a more specific name to take.
audit.rule.request-example.label: Request schema without an example
audit.rule.request-example.message: The {mediaType} request schema shows no example of a value to send.
audit.rule.request-example.why: Tools built from the operation copy the request schema whole, its examples included, and drop the media type's example and examples. An example written there prefills this documentation's try-it but never reaches an agent, which then fills the body from types alone: a string says nothing of the id format, the date layout or the unit the API expects.
audit.rule.request-example.fix: Move or copy the example onto the schema — example in OpenAPI 3.0, examples: [ … ] from 3.1 — or give each property an example of its own.
audit.rule.error-machine-readable.label: Error body an agent cannot read
audit.rule.error-machine-readable.messag: The {status} response describes its body as prose, with no field to read.
audit.rule.error-machine-readable.why: An agent whose call fails reads this body to decide what to do next: which field was refused, whether to retry, whether to ask the user. Text, HTML, or JSON without a schema leaves it a sentence to interpret, and it guesses or gives up on the task.
audit.rule.error-machine-readable.fix: Declare a JSON schema for the {status} body, ideally application/problem+json (RFC 9457) with type, title and detail, plus the fields a client branches on — the refused parameter, whether to retry.
audit.rule.server-https.label: Server over plain http
audit.rule.server-https.message: Requests to {url} travel unencrypted, and browsers block them from any https page.
audit.rule.server-https.why: A server URL with http:// sends every request in clear: tokens, passwords, API keys and payloads can be read and altered by anyone on the network path. Browsers also block a request from an https page to an http address as mixed content, so the try-it of any documentation served over https cannot reach this server, and says so. localhost, 127.0.0.1 and [::1] are exempt: browsers trust them, and the request never leaves the machine.
audit.rule.server-https.fix: Serve the API over https and write the URL with https://. Keep http:// only for a localhost development server.
audit.rule.oauth-url-tls.label: OAuth endpoint over plain http
audit.rule.oauth-url-tls.message: The {field} {url} is plain http; OAuth requires TLS on every endpoint of the authorization server.
audit.rule.oauth-url-tls.why: RFC 6749 requires TLS on the authorization endpoint (§3.1) and the token endpoint (§3.2), and refresh tokens travel only over TLS (§10.4); the device endpoint (RFC 8628 §3.1), the authorization server metadata (RFC 8414 §3) and the OpenID Connect discovery document require https too. Over http, the user's password, the authorization code, the client secret and the tokens cross the network in clear. From an https page, the try-it's login sends the reader to that http page, and the browser blocks a token request to http as mixed content.
audit.rule.oauth-url-tls.fix: Serve the authorization server over https and write {field} with https://.
audit.rule.auth-scheme-weak.label: Credential sent over plain http
audit.rule.auth-scheme-weak.message: This operation sends its “{scheme}” credential to {url}, a plain http server.
audit.rule.auth-scheme-weak.why: A credential sent without TLS can be read on the network path and replayed. RFC 6750 §5.3 requires TLS on every request carrying a bearer token, OAuth access tokens included; RFC 7617 §4 says Basic authentication, a password in clear, should not be used without it; a mutualTLS client certificate travels in the TLS handshake (RFC 8705 §2), so over http that scheme cannot work at all. Basic is a warning, bearer tokens and mutualTLS are errors.
audit.rule.auth-scheme-weak.fix: Serve the operation over https, or remove the http:// server from the servers it lists.
audit.rule.apikey-in-query.label: API key in the query string
audit.rule.apikey-in-query.message: The API key “{name}” travels in the URL, which servers and proxies log in full.
audit.rule.apikey-in-query.why: A URL is not a secret: servers, proxies, CDNs and load balancers log it whole, and a browser that opens it keeps it in its history. TLS does not help, the URL is logged in clear at both ends. RFC 9110 §17.9 calls sensitive information in a URI unwise, RFC 6750 §2.3 says a token should not go in a query parameter when a header can carry it, and OWASP API2:2023 lists credentials in the URL as broken authentication.
audit.rule.apikey-in-query.fix: Accept the key in a header (in: header, X-API-Key for instance), and keep the query form only as a deprecated alternative for existing clients.
audit.rule.http-scheme-registered.label: Unregistered HTTP authentication scheme
audit.rule.http-scheme-registered.messag: “{scheme}” is not a registered HTTP authentication scheme: it goes out as the first word of the Authorization header, and a server expecting Bearer refuses it.
audit.rule.http-scheme-registered.why: OpenAPI says the scheme of an http security scheme should be registered with IANA (Basic, Bearer, Digest, DPoP…), compared without case. It is not a label: clients send it as the first word of the Authorization header. The try-it sends it in lowercase and the exported MCP config capitalized, so “JWT” goes out as “jwt <token>” and “Jwt <token>”, and a value with a space breaks the header.
audit.rule.http-scheme-registered.fix: For a token, use scheme: bearer with bearerFormat: JWT; for a key in a custom header, an apiKey scheme with in: header.
audit.rule.operation-unsecured.label: Operation callable without credentials
audit.rule.operation-unsecured.message: No credentials are required here: no security requirement applies, or one lets anonymous callers in.
audit.rule.operation-unsecured.why: OWASP API2:2023 (Broken Authentication) starts with an endpoint that does not check who calls it. The document is the contract: a client generated from it sends no credential, and this documentation shows no authentication section and a try-it with no credentials form. Open by omission is a warning on a method that changes state and a note on a read; a security: [] at the root counts as an omission, since generators write it by default. Open by declaration (security: [] on the operation, or an empty {} alternative) is a note, the list of what is public on purpose. A document with no scheme and no security anywhere gets a single finding.
audit.rule.operation-unsecured.fix: Declare a scheme under components.securitySchemes and the security requirement the operation needs, at the root or on the operation. If it is public on purpose, say so with security: [] on the operation — an operation already declared public needs nothing more.
audit.rule.secured-op-errors.label: Secured operation silent on refused credentials
audit.rule.secured-op-errors.message: Not documented: {missing}. A client is left to guess how this API refuses credentials and how to authenticate.
audit.rule.secured-op-errors.why: A client learns from the status that its credentials were refused: 401 means authenticate, and RFC 9110 §15.5.2 requires the server to send a WWW-Authenticate header naming the scheme with it; 403 means these credentials are not enough (§15.5.4). A generated client maps each documented status to an error, an agent reads them to decide whether to ask for credentials; undocumented, an expired token looks like a bug in the request. This documentation does not read WWW-Authenticate from a live response, so the document is where a reader learns it.
audit.rule.secured-op-errors.fix: Document a 401 response with a WWW-Authenticate header naming the scheme (Bearer for a bearer token), and a 403 where valid credentials can still be refused. Write them once under components.responses and reference them.
audit.rule.oauth-legacy-flows.label: OAuth flow the security best practice retires
audit.rule.oauth-legacy-flows.message: The OAuth 2.0 security best practice (RFC 9700) tells clients not to use the {flow} flow.
audit.rule.oauth-legacy-flows.why: The password flow hands the user's password to the client app, which sees it and sends it on: RFC 9700 §2.4 says it MUST NOT be used. The implicit flow returns the access token in the redirect URL, where it can leak and be replayed: §2.1.2 says clients SHOULD NOT use it. This documentation's try-it runs neither and falls back to a token pasted by hand.
audit.rule.oauth-legacy-flows.fix: Move clients to the authorizationCode flow with PKCE, or clientCredentials for a machine client, then remove the {flow} flow. Meanwhile, a scheme left with only that flow can be marked deprecated (OpenAPI 3.2).
audit.rule.rate-limit-retry-after.label: 429 response without Retry-After
audit.rule.rate-limit-retry-after.messag: This {status} response does not document a Retry-After header.
audit.rule.rate-limit-retry-after.why: RFC 6585 lets a 429 say how long to wait before the next request: a Retry-After header, in seconds or as an HTTP date (RFC 9110 §10.2.3). A client written without knowing it is there retries at once and stays throttled, or backs off by a guess. This documentation's try-it shows the delay from a live response either way, when the API exposes the header to the browser; only the document tells a client's author before the first 429.
audit.rule.rate-limit-retry-after.fix: Declare a Retry-After header on the 429 response (an integer of seconds, or an HTTP date) and send it. Several operations sharing the response: declare it once under components.responses.
audit.rule.sensitive-field-exposure.mess: A response returns this password (format: password): it is not marked writeOnly, the keyword OpenAPI and JSON Schema give a value that is sent but never returned.
audit.rule.sensitive-field-exposure.why: The schema says the API hands the secret back to whoever reads the resource: OWASP API3:2023 lists exposing properties that should not be read as broken authorization. writeOnly is the keyword for a value the client sends and never gets back: OpenAPI 3.0 says it should not be sent in a response, JSON Schema 2020-12 (§9.4) that it is never present when the instance is retrieved. Generated clients type the response with the field, and this documentation's response sample shows it filled in, where a writeOnly property is left out.
audit.rule.sensitive-field-exposure.fix: Mark the property writeOnly: true and keep the value out of the API's responses. If the response really returns a secret, such as an API key shown once at creation, drop format: password there and say so in the description.
audit.rule.unbounded-input.label: Inputs with no size limit
audit.rule.unbounded-input.message: Inputs of this operation with no maximum size: {names} ({count} in all). OWASP asks for a maximum length on every string and a maximum count on every array an API accepts.
audit.rule.unbounded-input.why: OWASP API4:2023 (Unrestricted Resource Consumption) puts it first among the preventions: a maximum length for strings and a maximum number of elements for arrays, on every parameter and payload. A limit the server enforces but the document does not state is one every client finds by failing, and a gateway validating against the schema lets any size through. A string counts as bounded by maxLength, an enum or const, a fixed-shape format (date, date-time, time, uuid, ipv4, ipv6, duration) or a pattern anchored with ^ and $ that repeats nothing without limit; an array by maxItems, an enum or const, or prefixItems with items: false. Files, numbers and readOnly properties are not counted.
audit.rule.unbounded-input.fix: Add maxLength to the strings and maxItems to the arrays among {names}, at the values the server enforces.
